UPSTREAM: kvm: x86: make lapic hrtimer pinned When a vCPU runs on a nohz_full core, the hrtimer used by the lapic emulation code can be migrated to another core. When this happens, it's possible to observe milisecond latency when delivering timer IRQs to KVM guests. The huge latency is mainly due to the fact that apic_timer_fn() expects to run during a kvm exit. It sets KVM_REQ_PENDING_TIMER and let it be handled on kvm entry. However, if the timer fires on a different core, we have to wait until the next kvm exit for the guest to see KVM_REQ_PENDING_TIMER set. This problem became visible after commit 9642d18ee. This commit changed the timer migration code to always attempt to migrate timers away from nohz_full cores. While it's discussable if this is correct/desirable (I don't think it is), it's clear that the lapic emulation code has a requirement on firing the hrtimer in the same core where it was started. This is achieved by making the hrtimer pinned. Lastly, note that KVM has code to migrate timers when a vCPU is scheduled to run in different core. However, this forced migration may fail. When this happens, we can have the same problem. If we want 100% correctness, we'll have to modify apic_timer_fn() to cause a kvm exit when it runs on a different core than the vCPU. Not sure if this is possible. Here's a reproducer for the issue being fixed: 1. Set all cores but core0 to be nohz_full cores 2. Start a guest with a single vCPU 3. Trace apic_timer_fn() and kvm_inject_apic_timer_irqs() You'll see that apic_timer_fn() will run in core0 while kvm_inject_apic_timer_irqs() runs in a different core. If you get both on core0, try running a program that takes 100% of the CPU and pin it to core0 to force the vCPU out. Signed-off-by: Luiz Capitulino <lcapitulino@redhat.com> Signed-off-by: Paolo Bonzini <pbonzini@redhat.com> BUG=b:120040011 TEST=Built (cherry picked from commit 61abdbe0bcc2b32745ab4479cc550f4c1f518ee2) Signed-off-by: Matt Delco <delco@chromium.org> Signed-off-by: Dmitry Torokhov <dtor@chromium.org> Change-Id: I8cba95cfab9fa60c24040e972ca67cf6fb9608a0 Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/1762320 Legacy-Commit-Queue: Commit Bot <commit-bot@chromium.org> Reviewed-by: Sean Paul <seanpaul@chromium.org>

touch_updater: stupdate updater now uses common rebind_driver() function. Previously this updater script had its own rebind implementation, probably because rebind_driver() used to not support binding a device which didn't successfuly bind on boot, e.g. because its firmware was corrupt. This now takes advantage of being able to specify the driver to (re)bind the device to. BUG=b:132830741 TEST=Tested no-update, normal update, and firmware corruption recovery with stupdate touch updater. All cases succeeded as expected. Verified by testing basic touch functionality, examining /var/log/messages, and querying the touch controller for its firmware version. UPSTREAM: r8152: Add support for MAC address pass through on RTL8153-BND All previous docks and dongles that have supported this feature use the RTL8153-AD chip. RTL8153-BND is a new chip that will be used in upcoming Dell type-C docks. It should be added to the whitelist of devices to activate MAC address pass through. Per confirming with Realtek all devices containing RTL8153-BND should activate MAC pass through and there won't use pass through bit on efuse like in RTL8153-AD. mount-encrypted: add the new cmdline option "insecure" mount-encrypted doesn't store an insecure system key in NVRAM, which allows us to keep encstateful not wiped over TPM clearing and avoids potential unexpected behavior caused by soft-clearing TPM 2.0. The option should only be enabled for testing purposes and will be used in the autotest env. This CL provdes an alternative and simpler way to solve the soft-clearing TPM 2.0 problem mentioned above, compared with the original solution in CL:1753389. BUG=b:139399088 TEST=tested along with CL:1763468: On a chell, make sure the changes are no-op in any case. On a soraka, create the magic file in /mnt/stateful_partition, then 1. Run crossystem to clear the TPM, reboot, and log in. Then, repeat those 3 steps a few times and make sure each time the encrypted partition is not wiped. Also, check if mount-encrypted.log says it uses an insecure system key. 2. Run tpm_softclear to soft-clear the TPM, then run tpm_manager_client take_ownership to re-own the TPM, then reboot. Make sure the encrypted partition isn't wiped and mount-encrypted.log says it uses an insecure system key. 3. Remove the magic file, run crossystem to clear the TPM, reboot, and make sure the encrypted partition is wiped and mount-encrypted.log says it creates a random key and stores it in NVRAM. Change-Id: I68c762de6115ec33e3ea7ebc35f50f7264578b21 Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/1763467 Tested-by: Wei-Cheng Xiao <garryxiao@chromium.org> Commit-Ready: Wei-Cheng Xiao <garryxiao@chromium.org> Legacy-Commit-Queue: Commit Bot <commit-bot@chromium.org> Reviewed-by: Mattias Nissler <mnissler@chromium.org>

vm_tools: sommelier: A better fix for scaling The previous fix for scaling tried to undo some of the calculations made on the display, but only in the special case of the internal display, it had two drawbacks: - Two wrongs dont make a right - It didnt work for external displays with nonstandard DPI. This is a better fix which solves both problems by scrapping the physical size calculation and instead working backwards from the DPI we want to end up with (which comes from the ideal scale and the conventional DPI).
